column2: Also on the authority of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: “While we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ one day, there appeared before us a man whose clothes were exceedingly white and whose hair was exceedingly black. We could see no trace of travel on him, and none of us knew him,
until he sat down by the Prophet ﷺ,
rested his knees against his knees, placed his palms on his thighs, and said: O Muḥammad,
tell me about Islam. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Islam is that you testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah,
establish the prayer, give the zakāh, fast Ramaḍān, and make pilgrimage to the House if you are able to find a way to it. He said: You have spoken truly.

We were amazed at him: he asks him and then confirms him! He said: Then tell me about faith (īmān). He said: That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, and that you believe in the decree (qadar), its good and its bad. He said: You have spoken truly.

He said: Then tell me about excellence (iḥsān). He said: That you worship Allah as though you see Him; and though you do not see Him, He surely sees you. He said: Then tell me about the Hour. He said: The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking. He said: Then tell me about its signs.
He said: That the slave-woman gives birth to her mistress, and that you see the barefoot, unclothed, destitute shepherds of sheep competing in raising tall buildings.
Then he left, and we stayed a long while. Then he said: O ʿUmar, do you know who the questioner was?
I said: Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: That was Jibrīl, who came to you to teach you your religion.” Reported by Muslim.
Baynamā (“while”): an adverb of time conveying something sudden. Idh ṭalaʿa (“there appeared”): when there came into view.

Rajul (“a man”): he was in the form of a person of our kind. Athar al-safar (“trace of travel”): the marks of travel, such as dust and dishevelled hair. “We were amazed at him: he asks him and then confirms him”: we wondered at his affair,

since a questioner is supposed not to know what he asks about. Bi-l-qadar (“in the decree”): what Allah has measured out and decreed of good and evil. ʿAn al-sāʿah (“about the Hour”): about the establishment of the Hour. Amārātuhā (“its signs”): its indications that show it is coming.

Al-amah (“the slave-woman”): the woman who is owned. Rabbatahā (“her mistress”): her owner. Al-ḥufāh (“the barefoot”): plural of ḥāfin, one with no sandal on his foot. Al-ʿurāh (“the unclothed”): plural of ʿārin, one who has nothing on his body. Al-ʿālah (“the destitute”):

plural of ʿāʾil, the poor man. Riʿāʾ al-shāʾ (“shepherds of sheep”): herders of sheep. “Competing in raising tall buildings”: vying and boasting with one another in raising buildings high. Labithnā (“we stayed”): we remained. Malīyyan (“a long while”): a long time, said to be three days.
The gloss on malīyyan reads قبل ثلاثة أيام (“before three days”), evidently for قيل ثلاثة أيام (“said to be three days”).
The angels take on whatever forms they wish.
The etiquette of the learner and one seeking guidance with a scholar.
When Islam and faith are mentioned together, Islam is explained by outward deeds and faith by inward deeds.
Islam, faith and excellence are each called religion.
The Hour is among the matters whose knowledge Allah has kept to Himself: “Indeed, with Allah is knowledge of the Hour” [Luqmān 31:34].
Among the signs of the Hour are the abundance of concubines and their children, or children's undutifulness to their mothers, as though the mothers were slave-women to them.
The obligation to believe in the decree, and that one must be content with whatever good or bad Allah has decreed for a person.
A person should refrain from delving into matters of which he has no knowledge.
The dislike of making buildings tall and ornate beyond what need calls for.

The report that among the signs of the Hour is that worldly riches are opened up to the people of the desert and of poverty, so that their concerns turn to erecting buildings and they have no concern other than that.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him) informs us in this well-known hadith of Jibrīl that Jibrīl (peace be upon him) came out to them in the form of an unknown man while they were sitting with the Prophet ﷺ, and he sat before the Prophet ﷺ in the manner of a learner seeking guidance.

He asked him about Islam, faith and excellence, and he answered him with these pillars, which include affirming the two testimonies, keeping up the five prayers, paying the zakāh to those entitled to it, fasting the month of Ramaḍān with a sincere intention, performing the obligatory Ḥajj for whoever is able, and believing that Allah is the Creator and Provider, described by perfection and free of deficiency;

that the angels are honoured servants whom Allah created, who do not disobey Allah the Exalted and act by His command; believing in the books sent down to the messengers from Allah the Exalted, and in the messengers who conveyed His religion from Allah; and that a person should worship Allah as though he were beholding Him, Glorified is He,
and if he does not attain this worship, let him worship Allah the Exalted out of fear of Him, knowing that He is watching and that nothing is hidden from Him;

that none of the creation knows when the Hour will be; that among the signs of the Hour are an abundance of concubines and their children, or widespread undutifulness of children to their mothers, treating them as slave-women;
and that worldly riches will be spread out for the shepherds and the poor at the end of time, so they will vie with one another in ornamenting and erecting buildings.
All these questions and their answers were from Jibrīl, to teach this pure and upright religion, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “This was Jibrīl, who came to you to teach you your religion.”
A man is only where he places himself, / so place yourself among righteous deeds.
